content: This judgment from the Court of Nocera Inferiore First Civil Section addresses the procedural requirements for proving heir status in inheritance division proceedings. The plaintiff brought proceedings in 2015 to obtain judicial dissolution of joint ownership of inherited real estate following the death of her father. The defendant appeared objecting preliminarily to inadmissibility for failure to attempt mediation pursuant to Article 5 of Legislative Decree 28/2010, and on merits requested estate division. One defendant remained in default despite proper notification. During proceedings, the case was declared closed as to one party for failure to re-serve within court-set time limits. The court held that regardless of mediation objections, the case could be decided by applying the principle of the "most liquid reason" whereby decision may be based on logically subordinate issue suitable for defining judgment. The court noted that acceptance of division claim presupposes verification of title to succeed, which in legitimate succession consists of alleged family relationships with deceased and must necessarily be proven by civil status documents, specifically the full family status certificate for succession purposes, citing consistent Supreme Court jurisprudence. The plaintiff failed to produce the historical family certificate for inheritance purposes, the only document suitable for proving kinship degree between deceased and plaintiffs. The court acknowledged existence of interpretative approach requiring specific proof of kinship only when family relationship is disputed, so that absent objection the relationship should be considered established. However, the court rejected this approach, holding that rules governing intestate succession devolution are undoubtedly non-negotiable with clear public relevance linked to presence of Italian State as legitimate heir in supplementary position. This non-negotiable nature renders any non-contestation of heir status by parties completely irrelevant and requires judge to ascertain status ex officio. The court noted that Supreme Court jurisprudence recognizes that persons claiming heir status in succession to proceedings must prove such status by producing civil status documents regardless of whether contested, as this relates to proper constitution of adversarial process and mandatory public procedural law provisions. If succession title must be ascertained ex officio in procedural succession context, such verification is required a fortiori when plaintiff exercises right presupposing legitimate heir status, given same mandatory non-negotiable nature applies to substantive law rules governing intestate succession. The approach requiring ex officio verification without weight to non-contestation aims to prevent abuse through fictitious disputes to detriment of true legitimate heirs who may differ from parties who have not proved alleged status. The court also held proof of status cannot be given by applying non-contestation principle. These considerations led to rejection of dissolution application as inadmissible in absence of timely proper production of required documentation. Costs were fully compensated between parties given nature of dispute and reasons for decision. law: Divorce
